posts.author: Tommy
posts.content_md:
Will an LCD panel work without the polarizer?

My understanding is that a liquid crystal in the "off" state rotates the polarization of light passing through it 90 degrees, and that in the "on" position it does not rotate it. Thus only with the polarizers on each side of the LCD does that rotation become opaque or clear.

Or is your goal to be able to rotate the polarizers to whatever angle you want, since the liquid crystal's rotation action dosn't really have an inherent horizontal or vertical to it?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:4b2eebffa8]My understanding is that a liquid crystal in the "off" state rotates the polarization of light passing through it 90 degrees, and that in the "on" position it does not rotate it. [/quote:4b2eebffa8]

In a twisted pair nematic liquid crystal display, the first polariser is only to set the polarisation of the incoming light. The nematic liquid crystal is twisted so as to cause a polarisation change in the light, using the birefringence of the crystal. The polariser on the other side then allows or blocks the light dependant on the twist of the crystal, which is set by the E-field. This, of course, would be meaningless if the input light were not initially polarised by the first polariser

. Since the laser light is already polarised (assuming that it is - not all lasers are), the first polariser is then redundant. In fact, it might even be detrimental if the laser's polarisation were at an angle to the LCD's first polariser.

[http://chemistry.umeche.maine.edu/CHY132/LXDisplay.html](http://chemistry.umeche.maine.edu/CHY132/LXDisplay.html)

[quote:340f6beec2] As the angle increases, the reflectivity, and hence the glancing reflection, also increases.

You have 1/2w plates just laying around? Sure, I'll take one. 

 What I'd really like is to not even need it if possible. It's just another optic to scatter stray light and reduce the beam power. 

[/quote:340f6beec2] 

I think we've got two posts mixed up. The increase in reflectivity was referring to the Fresnel reflection off the emulsion side of the H1. It was regarding the comment about angles for H1 and H2. It had nothing to do with the twisted nematic liquid crystals.

When the reference hits the H1, some of it enters the emulsion and some of it reflects off the front surface of the emulsion. The exact amounts are of course index dependant and can be calculated using the Fresnel formula:

For 's' polarisation,

r(s) = (n*cos(theta_i)) - cos(theta_t))/(n*cos(theta_i)) + cos(theta_i)))

and for 'p' polarisation,

r(p) =(2*cos(theta_i))/(n*cos(theta_i)) + cos(theta_t)))

where n = index of emulsion

theta_i = incident angle of reference beam

theta_t = angle of reference beam inside emulsion. The transmission coefficants are given by:

t = 1-r

(Hope all the brackets add up, it's difficult to write out in 'full'!)

From these you can see that the steeper the incident angle, the greater is r and therefore the less is t. It's then straightforward to incorporate this into the desired beam ratio and calculate the desired H1 reference angle.

As for the LCD point, sure, you can use a 1/2 wave plate to make the polarisation of the laser correspond with the transmission axis of the first polariser on the LCD. However, as you say, this increases the possibility of stray reflections. It's far easier to take advantage of the fact that the laser is already polarised and take off the first polariser. How you'd do it, I have no idea. I know how I'd do it. I'd give it to Joy and say "Take the stupid polariser off!"

Bear in mind that phase retardations by the nematic liquid are wavelength dependant, as are all phase retardations in a birefringent material.

posts.content_md:
I never found any information on removing the polarizer on an LCD panel so I decided to experiment on my own this morning.

It turns out to be pretty easy with the particular Sharp color panel I'm working with.

I just picked at one corner of the "something" that was on one surface of the panel (given that another panel actually had multiple flexible overlays for each color, I couldn't be 100% sure that I was picking at a polarizer on this one) and carefully lifted up the corner until I could tell if a semi-clear sheet was coming off or if a color overlay was being lifted up.

Turns out it was the former and I kept lifting very carefully. The sheet was stuck down with an adhesive that wasn't much different from rubber cement and was still flexible. Still, I had to go slow as it took a fair amount of force to lift the sheet off and I didn't want to break the glass. To ease some of the pressure I started cutting the sheet so I could pull off thin strips until I had all of the polarizer off.

I was a little worried at first because I couldn't see any image at all after doing this but found that if I put one of the pieces of polarizer back on the glass (it was quite sticky on one side) that the image from my second "monitor" showed up just fine.

Next I turned on one of my many spare lasers and shone some light through the panel. Hmmm. Not so good. The image shows a bizarre diffraction pattern. How about if I put a diffuser behind the panel. Worse, the image disappears. How about if I put the diffuser in front of the panel (between me and the panel). Hey! That gives me a nice bright image!

I'll post some photos when I get the chance but since this is the first time I've had time away from work to make some holograms I'm going to put another piece of film on the table and work on the PCGGI videos while that settles.
